title: Does ‘Judge Not’ Mean Christians Can’t Say Anything Is Wrong?
subtitle: Jesus said it to disciples he expected to correct one another. What the speck and the beam forbid, what they require, and why the verse is neither a weapon nor a gag.

sections.title: The Verse That Ends Arguments
sections.body:
Plenty of people who couldn't name another Bible verse can quote this one. In the King James wording it's two words, judge not, and they turn up on T-shirts, in comment threads, and at family dinners whenever someone calls something wrong. The Berean Standard Bible renders it “Do not judge, or you will be judged” (Matthew 7:1). It's usually said to end an argument, and it usually does.

People reach for it for reasons that deserve respect, and many learned it on the receiving end. They were whispered about in a church lobby after a divorce, an arrest, or a relapse. They heard sermons against sins the preacher had no taste for, and some watched a leader who condemned others turn out to be doing what he condemned. When someone like that quotes Jesus at a harsh Christian, he isn't twisting the Bible. He's often aiming it exactly where Jesus did, since it was first said to people who meant to follow him, about how they would treat each other. The skeptic who has noticed that Christians can be severe with every sin but their own has noticed something true, and the verse is on his side. I'm a pastor, and part of my work is telling people when something is wrong, so this passage was aimed at me first.

But the verse has a second life, as a way to close every moral conversation before it starts, as though Jesus had said nothing may ever be called wrong. Used that way, it silences more than harshness. It silences the person who needed someone to say out loud that what was done to them was wrong. It deserves better than both, and the way to give it better is to read it where Jesus said it, with its paragraph still attached.

sections.title: The Sermon Around the Sentence
sections.body:
The verse sits near the end of the Sermon on the Mount, the teaching Matthew gathers in chapters 5 to 7. Jesus had been preaching and healing across Galilee, around AD 30, with crowds following him from as far as Jerusalem and the Decapolis (4:25). Seeing them, he went up on the mountain, sat down, and taught his disciples while the crowds listened (5:1-2; 7:28).

Before it reaches our verse, the sermon has staked a great deal on mercy: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy” (Matthew 5:7). Chapter 6 teaches a prayer that asks, “And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” (Matthew 6:12), the only petition Jesus stops to explain (6:14-15).

Then comes the paragraph: “Do not judge, or you will be judged. For with the same judgment you pronounce, you will be judged; and with the measure you use, it will be measured to you” (Matthew 7:1-2). A question follows, with a joke inside it: “Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?” (7:3). Then the remedy: “You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye” (7:5).

The next sentence requires a judgment: “Do not give dogs what is holy; do not throw your pearls before swine” (7:6). Soon after comes a warning, “Beware of false prophets. They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (7:15), and a way to tell them apart: “By their fruit you will recognize them” (7:16).

Luke's shorter version sets the saying right after “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36) and gives it two companions that show which judging is meant: “Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). The speck and the beam follow (6:41-42).

sections.title: A Speck, a Beam, and a Brother
sections.body:
The first hearers were Galilean fishermen and villagers (4:18-22), people who knew the Law and bought their grain by the measure. The Law forbade keeping “two differing measures in your house, one large and one small” (Deuteronomy 25:14), and Jewish teachers spoke of God repaying people measure for measure, a principle later written down in the Mishnah around AD 200. Jesus turns it on the one doing the judging: the measure you use on your neighbor is the one God will use on you, a warning to the harsh and a promise to the merciful.

Then the picture turns absurd, on purpose. A speck is a chip of straw or wood; a beam is a roof timber. A man with a beam in his eye leans in to operate on his brother's: “How can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ while there is still a beam in your own eye?” (7:4). The speck is real. The judge is wrong about himself, not his brother, and his offer of help is a performance. The Greek word behind hypocrite was the ordinary word for an actor, and the sermon has already used it three times for people who give, pray, and fast to be seen (6:2, 5, 16). The judge is playing the righteous man, and the part needs an audience.

The grammar closes in, too: verses 1 and 2 are plural, but from verse 3 on the you is singular, and no one in the crowd could hear it as a word about someone else.

Nor does the paragraph end by telling anyone to leave his brother alone. It ends with a clear eye and a speck removed. What Jesus forbids is the order we prefer: speck first, beam never. Then he asks them to decide who the dogs and swine are, unclean animals to a Jewish ear, and to know wolves by their fruit. Interpreters still disagree about whom the animals stand for, but no one can obey that verse without judging. Its first hearers could not have taken verse 1 to mean that nothing may be named.

sections.title: What It Forbids, and What It Doesn't
sections.body:
The verse still forbids what it forbade on that hillside. It forbids the judgment that exempts itself, measuring others by a standard we never apply to ourselves. It forbids merciless judgment, which the letter of James warns will be answered in kind (James 2:13). And it forbids taking God's seat. We can see what people do, but only God sees the heart (1 Samuel 16:7), so verdicts on motives and final destinies are his: “Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes” (1 Corinthians 4:5).

It doesn't forbid discernment, calling sin sin, or correcting one another; the same Jesus says, “Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly” (John 7:24).

The verse has been misread from both ends. Some of us who follow Jesus have used truth as a weapon, severe with the world's sins and gentle with our own, performing our outrage for audiences that already agree, which is the actor's part Jesus named. Paul expected the church to judge inside its own household and leave outsiders to God (1 Corinthians 5:12-13). We have often reversed the order.

Much of the culture has made the verse a gag, for fair reasons: people who no longer agree about the good life want a truce, and no one wants to be reduced to the worst thing he has done. But a truce in which nothing may be called wrong leaves the defrauded and the abused with no one to name what was done to them, and some churches have used this very verse to hush people who reported a leader's abuse. Nor has the culture stopped judging. It has kept the verdicts and lost the forgiveness.

Most of us keep verse 1 for our friends and verse 16 for our enemies. On the right, that has often meant patience with a favored leader and fruit inspection for everyone else; on the left, patience with whatever the movement approves and little mercy for anyone who crosses it. Those are the two measures the Law forbade, and I can find both in my own house.

sections.title: Beam First
sections.body:
Begin with the beam, and expect it to be hard to find. The social psychologist Jonathan Haidt argues in The Righteous Mind that moral judgment arrives first as intuition, with reasoning following to argue its case, and that the morality binding a group together also blinds it. From the inside, a beam doesn't feel like a beam. It feels like seeing clearly. Haidt describes a mechanism; Jesus names a sin, a harder word and a more hopeful one, since sin can be confessed and forgiven. Ask for help: “Who can discern his own errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (Psalm 19:12). A verdict that comes fast and hot is worth suspecting: David declared that a man deserved to die before learning that the man in Nathan's story was David (2 Samuel 12:5-7).

When a brother sins against you, go to him instead of around him, privately first (Matthew 18:15), with your own weakness in view: “restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted” (Galatians 6:1). Name what is wrong, and leave the verdict on the person to God.

Harm is a different matter, and no one who is afraid should go alone to the person who hurt them. If this verse has been used to keep you quiet about harm, it was misused; naming harm is not the judging Jesus forbade. Tell someone you trust, and if you or anyone else is in danger, call the police. And if you've been on the wrong end of Christian judgment, harsh and public and merciless, the sharpest word in this passage was spoken on your behalf.

Only one person on that hillside had clear eyes, and he was the one speaking. The Father has given him all judgment (John 5:22), and he was not sent “to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him” (John 3:17). The only judge without a beam went to a cross for people who had them. Every verdict you pass this week is a measure you will meet again. The verse doesn't ask you to put the measure down. It asks what you want to find in it when it comes back.
